title: Grammar Bank - Final 16 (B1-B2+)
instructions: Choose the correct word or phrase to complete the sentence.

items.question: I _____ in this city since I graduated from college five years ago.
items.explanation: The present perfect is used for an action that started in the past and continues into the present, especially with 'since'.

incorrectOptionExplanations.A: Simple present is for routines, not actions spanning from the past to now.
incorrectOptionExplanations.B: Present continuous is for temporary actions happening right now.
incorrectOptionExplanations.D: Past continuous implies an interrupted action in the past.

items.teachingTip: Remind students that 'since' + a specific point in the past almost always triggers the present perfect.
items.exampleSentence: She has worked at this company since 2021.

items.question: The new booking software is much _____ to use than the old one.
items.explanation: For two-syllable adjectives ending in 'y', change the 'y' to 'i' and add 'er' to form the comparative.

incorrectOptionExplanations.A: 'More easy' is grammatically incorrect; 'easy' takes the '-er' suffix.
incorrectOptionExplanations.C: Superlative is used for three or more things, but here we are comparing two (new vs. old).
incorrectOptionExplanations.D: This is an adverb, but we need an adjective to describe the software.

items.teachingTip: Have students practice spotting the word 'than', which is a huge clue that a comparative form is needed.
items.exampleSentence: This exercise is easier than the one we did yesterday.

items.question: You _____ wear a tie to the office, but it is highly recommended for important client meetings.
items.explanation: 'Don't have to' shows a lack of obligation (it's optional).

incorrectOptionExplanations.A: 'Mustn't' means it is forbidden, which contradicts the second half of the sentence.
incorrectOptionExplanations.C: 'Shouldn't' is advice against doing it, but the sentence says it's recommended.
incorrectOptionExplanations.D: 'Can't' means you lack the ability or permission.

items.grammarOrVocabularyFocus: Modals of Obligation / Lack of Obligation (B1)
items.teachingTip: Draw a clear distinction between 'mustn't' (prohibited) and 'don't have to' (your choice) as students constantly mix these up.
items.exampleSentence: You don't have to attend the seminar, but it would be good for your career.

items.question: If the traffic is bad this afternoon, I _____ you to let you know I'll be late.
items.explanation: The first conditional uses 'if + present simple, will + base verb' for real, possible future situations.

incorrectOptionExplanations.A: Missing 'will' for the future result clause.
incorrectOptionExplanations.C: 'Would call' is for the second conditional (unreal/hypothetical situations).
incorrectOptionExplanations.D: Present continuous is for planned future arrangements, not conditional results.

items.teachingTip: Show students the 'If X happens, Y will happen' formula as a concrete math equation to memorize.
items.exampleSentence: If I pass the MET, I will apply to that university.

items.question: She decided _____ a new language before her six-month trip to Japan.
items.explanation: The verb 'decide' is always followed by an infinitive with 'to'.

incorrectOptionExplanations.D: 'For' + gerund is used to explain the purpose of an object, not after 'decide'.

items.teachingTip: Group verbs logically for students: verbs about plans and choices (decide, plan, hope, want) usually take the infinitive.
items.exampleSentence: We decided to delay the project until next quarter.

items.question: By the time we arrived at the conference, the keynote speaker _____ her presentation.
items.explanation: The past perfect (had + past participle) is used to show that one action in the past happened before another action in the past.

incorrectOptionExplanations.A: Simple past doesn't clearly establish the sequence of which action happened first.
incorrectOptionExplanations.C: Present perfect cannot be used when the narrative is entirely in the past.
incorrectOptionExplanations.D: Past continuous means it was happening simultaneously, but 'already' implies completion.

items.teachingTip: Draw a timeline on the screen: Action 1 (speaker finished) happens before Action 2 (we arrived). Action 1 gets the Past Perfect.
items.exampleSentence: By the time I got to the station, the train had already left.

items.question: The updated company policies _____ to all employees by the end of the week.
items.explanation: The sentence requires the future passive voice because the policies receive the action (they are being sent by someone).

incorrectOptionExplanations.B: Active voice. Policies cannot send themselves.
incorrectOptionExplanations.C: Present continuous active voice. Incorrect meaning.
incorrectOptionExplanations.D: Present perfect active voice. Incorrect meaning.

items.teachingTip: Ask the student: 'Who is doing the action?' If the subject isn't doing the action, they need a passive structure (Be + Past Participle).
items.exampleSentence: The results will be published next Monday.

items.question: The manager _____ office is at the end of the hall can help you with that software issue.
items.explanation: 'Whose' is a relative pronoun used to show possession (the office belongs to the manager).

incorrectOptionExplanations.A: Used for the subject of a clause, not possession.
incorrectOptionExplanations.B: Used for the object of a clause, not possession.
incorrectOptionExplanations.D: Used for things, not people or possession.

items.teachingTip: Tell students that if they can replace the blank with 'his' or 'her' in two separate sentences, they need 'whose' to link them.
items.exampleSentence: She is the student whose essay won the competition.

items.question: The client called this morning and asked me when _____ the final report.
items.explanation: In reported questions, 'will' shifts back to 'would', and the word order changes from question format to statement format (subject + verb).

incorrectOptionExplanations.A: Incorrect question word order and failure to backshift 'will'.
incorrectOptionExplanations.C: Backshifts correctly to 'would', but uses question word order.
incorrectOptionExplanations.D: Uses statement word order, but fails to backshift 'will' to 'would'.

items.teachingTip: Remind students that reported questions are not actually questions anymore—they are statements. Therefore, no inverted word order.
items.exampleSentence: She asked me where I was going.

items.question: If they had known about the budget cuts earlier, they _____ the new marketing project.
items.explanation: The third conditional is used for past unreal situations. Formula: If + past perfect, would have + past participle.

incorrectOptionExplanations.A: This is second conditional (for present/future unreal situations).
incorrectOptionExplanations.B: Simple past doesn't form a conditional result clause.

items.teachingTip: Use the concept of 'regrets' or 'changing the past' to explain the third conditional's purpose.
items.exampleSentence: If I had studied harder, I would have passed the exam.

items.question: We need to _____ a solution to this supply chain problem before the board meeting tomorrow.
items.explanation: 'Come up with' means to invent, create, or think of an idea or solution.

incorrectOptionExplanations.C: Means to escape punishment for doing something wrong.
incorrectOptionExplanations.D: Means to be excited about a future event.

items.teachingTip: Teach three-part phrasal verbs in chunks with a common collocated noun (e.g., come up with an idea/solution).
items.exampleSentence: She came up with a brilliant marketing strategy.

items.question: Rarely _____ such dedication from a new employee during their first month on the job.
items.explanation: When negative or restrictive adverbs (rarely, seldom, never) are placed at the beginning of a sentence for emphasis, subject-auxiliary inversion is required.

incorrectOptionExplanations.A: Lacks the required inversion (should be 'have we seen').
incorrectOptionExplanations.C: Standard word order; incorrect after 'Rarely' at the start of a sentence.

items.teachingTip: Tell students that starting with a negative adverb forces the sentence to behave like a question structurally (auxiliary before subject).
items.exampleSentence: Never have I ever seen such a beautiful sunset.

items.question: By next December, I _____ for this organization for exactly a decade.
items.explanation: The future perfect continuous is used to emphasize the duration of an action up to a specific point in the future. ('Will have worked' is also grammatically possible, but continuous is preferred for ongoing employment duration).

incorrectOptionExplanations.A: Future continuous focuses on an action in progress at a time, not the accumulated duration.
incorrectOptionExplanations.B: Possible, but less natural than continuous when emphasizing the 'exactly a decade' duration of an ongoing action.
incorrectOptionExplanations.D: Conditional 'would' does not fit a definite future timeline.

items.teachingTip: Look for the double time marker: 'By [future time]' + 'for [duration]'. This usually signals Future Perfect Continuous.
items.exampleSentence: By 5 PM, she will have been studying for six hours straight.

items.question: _____ by the overwhelmingly positive feedback, the development team worked through the weekend to launch the update early.
items.explanation: A past participle clause ('Encouraged by...') is used here to mean 'Because they were encouraged by...'.

incorrectOptionExplanations.A: Present participle means the team was doing the encouraging, but they received it.
incorrectOptionExplanations.B: Means the team encouraged someone else prior to working.
incorrectOptionExplanations.D: Infinitive of purpose. Means they worked through the weekend in order to encourage the feedback.

items.teachingTip: Show students how to unpack the clause to check meaning: 'Because they were encouraged = Encouraged'.
items.exampleSentence: Exhausted from the trip, he fell asleep immediately.

items.question: If he had accepted the promotion in London last year, he _____ much closer to his family right now.
items.explanation: This is a mixed conditional. The condition is in the past (If he had accepted), but the result is in the present (right now), requiring 'would + base verb'.

incorrectOptionExplanations.B: Third conditional result, which would mean the result was also in the past.
incorrectOptionExplanations.C: First conditional result, which clashes with the past condition.
incorrectOptionExplanations.D: Simple present does not convey the hypothetical nature of the result.

items.teachingTip: Have students hunt for time markers in conditional sentences. 'Last year' vs 'right now' is the giveaway that it's mixed.
items.exampleSentence: If I had eaten breakfast, I wouldn't be hungry now.

items.question: What _____ was not the delay itself, but the complete lack of communication from the airline staff.
items.explanation: This is a cleft sentence starting with 'What', used to focus on a specific part of a sentence. Structure: What + subject/verb + is/was...

incorrectOptionExplanations.B: Unnecessary use of 'did' for emphasis in a structure that is already emphatic.
incorrectOptionExplanations.C: Passive voice is incorrect here; the delay is what caused the frustration.

items.teachingTip: Translate the cleft sentence back to a normal sentence to show how it works: 'The lack of communication frustrated me most' -> 'What frustrated me most was...'
items.exampleSentence: What I need right now is a good cup of coffee.
